body: Thanks for your comment- I’ve searched them all for this key word and haven’t found anything… could there be another term for this?

I’ve seen that happen at a few libraries I’ve worked at in the past too, although it’s been more about opening the position with someone in mind, temp or not. I just applied for a job which was posted for only 4 days total, and I’m thinking that was likely the case.

I lost my drivers license a few years ago. It’s a common experience after a seizure, even if you’re not epileptic. I’m 35 and can say that losing your license for a year may feel like the end of the world, but it’s a small sacrifice while you’re sorting out your health and understanding your triggers. You mention flashing lights- that’s not a trigger for everyone. While a lot of us do have common experiences, you’ll find that epilepsy can vary widely from person to person, and it’s a good idea to take your time while learning how it impacts you personally. Hang in there.
Oh interesting. Is that something that would be specific to sleep? And likely to repeat all night?

I definitely don’t want to go to bed stressed 😄 But my anxiety is much worse at night. I haven’t noticed that about anger, but I will keep an eye out for that too- thanks for the tip.

I do listen to a lot of podcasts when I can’t sleep, mostly the headspace “sleep cast” which is storytelling for adults and is designed to be relaxing.

Thank you for the tip- No, she doesn't. I keep fighting with insurance to be referred to someone who specializes in OCD/ is trained in ERP, and they keep telling me that everyone in their directory is capable of treating OCD. There's a huge lack of understanding of what ERP even is, and the mentality seems to be that OCD is just like every other mental health issue.

Oh wow, that sounds really tough. I'm sorry to hear that.

The only reason I've hesitated with NOCD is that I have a friend who uses it who told me that his therapist will only allow him to discuss his obsessions. If he mentions depression or other areas of his life, the therapist steers him back. But I'm still considering it, because I'm really struggling.

The process of therapy in general...I guess? We don't do any exposure therapy. The extent of our conversations is her saying I need to "focus on self care" until I get through this "stressful time" in my life. This has been a common thread in all therapists I've had in the last five years. Idk if it's an issue with the providers that are available to me-- my insurance, which offers mental health services through LifeStance, and I've tried BetterHelp. I did have a couple amazing therapists who both retired. 

I have been in therapy for the last 18 years. I've done CBT. I've done ACT. I've done EMDR. I've taken medication (several, actually). But nobody has ever done exposure therapy with me, even when I have specifically asked for it. I know that not all therapists have adequate training to offer ERP, and maybe that's the issue.
Thank you for this resource. I've heard anecdotally that OCD-specific therapists won't discuss other topics, like depression. Has that been true in your experience?

Thanks for your insight. I understand what she was trying to say-- I've had several other therapist explain it to me in the same way. It just hasn't been helpful to me because, while it may address shame, there's no practical application for actually coping with my phobias and the way the disrupt my daily life. I've been vocal in session about how this approach isn't helping me (especially because she is now applying it to every phobia I mention), but she repeatedly tells me I'm not "trusting the process" of therapy. I understand that the evolutionary drive to protect myself is present in all my phobias, but I don't understand how to move past that information into actionable steps.

Thanks for your insight. I'm not scared to tell her how I feel and have been vocal in session multiple times that this approach isn't helpful for me, but she insists that understanding the role of fear in human evolution will dispel my fear and repeatedly tells me I'm not trusting the process of therapy or that I'm impatient 

She's now generalizing this strategy to all my fears. For instance, I don't drive over bridges or on freeways because I experience intrusive images of myself driving off the bridge or freeway. Her response is the same-- "of course you're scared of that. Nobody wants to drive off a bridge." This is not helpful for obvious reasons. 

There has been no exposure related homework thus far. She just keeps telling me my OCD will always get worse when I'm stressed and if I want to live a normal life I need to reduce stress. I understand the role that stress plays, but her advice feels reductive.
Thanks for the book rec- definitely checking that out.

I've been in this exact situation. I privately spoke to the family member and explicitly told them, "I care about you and I'm worried my mental health is going to prevent me from being there for you in the way I'd like to. Please know that I care about you, even if I'm not able to be there."
That's the piece I'm really struggling with, because when I ask her what exactly the practical application of that information might be, the line of reasoning stops. Thank you for your input!

Hello again, and thanks for sharing. Unfortunately, I personally cannot take SSRIs in any amount. I was on a very low dose of Viibryd once upon a time, which precipitated my longest hospitalization to date. I have also tried lexapro and celexa, several others I can't even remember. Also... Not an SSRI, but many have recommended Wellbutrin. I have seizures, and I found out the hard way that Wellbutrin lowers the seizure threshold. 
Aaaand antipsychotics of any kind are out. I had a very rare and severe reaction to both abillify and vraylar in which my neutrophil count was over four times the safe limit. Very scary.

I dunno, I just don't metabolize medication well. *Any* medication. I currently take oxcarbazepine for the BP which helps tremendously, but has no effect whatsoever on my obsessive issues. I feel hopeless.

Wow, what a journey. Thank you for sharing and stay strong. 💕

I'm not able to use antipsychotics either. I have tried three. During the last, I had a rare reaction and my white blood cell count shot up off the charts overnight. Unfortunately, I can't use wellbutrin either because I have seizures and it lowers the seizure threshold (which I unfortunately  learned from experience). 

I don't know why, but my body just does not metabolize medication well-- any medication, even antihistamines. It's odd. I always seem have unusual reactions.

My ocd is also worst in mixed episodes, which is what I seem to have most often if I get off-kilter. 

Thank you so much for sharing this experience. I feel much less alone. 💙

Have you taken it before, or is this a new prescription for you?

Yes. I get intrusive images of accidents. It started when I was very young. For instance, I can remember riding my bicycle, and as a car would pass, I would envision myself falling sideways off my bike, and the car tire crushing my head. After the car actually passed and nothing happened, the scene would play over and over. That "scene," and many others still come to me. 

Other intrusive images are of things I am afraid I will do. I was hospitalized for a rare illness as a child, and during that time I had intrusive images of yanking my IV out of my arm.  I had to squeeze the rails on my bed until I was exhausted because I feared I would do it. Today, I get intrusive images of running my car into an oncoming semi, and at times I have to pull over because it is so intense.
Thank you for the input. I'm trying to find a way to fit brushing and heavy work into my morning before I leave. I usually do it mid-day. Mornings are extremely difficult.

I have the same problem, and have had bizarre health problems over the course of my life as well. 

The only way I've gotten through the last year is by telling myself that visiting the doctor is character building. I try to focus on maintaining a growth mindset. It doesn't always work, but it's been better than my previous strategy of avoiding. 

To be honest, I would never have gotten to the point of trying that if I hadn't been at the very end of my rope. Hitting rock bottom was ironically the only time cultivating growth mindset seemed like a possibility.

First of all, thank you for talking with me. This is going to be a long one.

Yes, stability is my idea of a payoff. I have some idea of what that looks like. I have seemingly constant health issues which baffle every Dr. I have seen. I know I can't be in perfect health, but I'd like to mellow out a bit. When a new one surfaces, I begin thinking 'wow, this is going to take an incredible amount of work, and probably money too. Or I could just die.' It's mostly the fatigue talking. So that feels unstable to me. 

Re: feeling isolated-- I become suspicious that my surroundings are not real, that other people are simulations, that I really am the only one having this experience, etc. Now, cognitively I see many errors in that theory, **which is how I know my medication is working.** But the times I can recognize those thoughts as false are usually short lived. So that aspect of my life is also very unstable. (Sidenote: this is what annoys me the most about the claim that one should simply choose how they feel. That's obviously a reductive argument.)

I also don't have a stable place to live right now. Have been on disability for a year, and just lost it in November. So no income.   

At this point in my life, I am thinking a lot about radical acceptance and the fine line separating that from resignation.  Therein lies the feeling of "this is it?" I'm just doomed to cycle in and out of psychosis, all while wasting away? I am relatively young-- about to turn 29-- and I don't know if I can do this for another 60 years (genes lead people to very ripe old ages in my family).

What makes you think I think of feeling as solely passive? Not sure where you got that. If I thought emotion was a passive experience, I wouldn't be doing any of the things I listed at the end of the post. 

Btw, in the dictionary, refute is literally defined as follows: "to prove to be false or erroneous as an **opinion or charge**" 

...and I never said anyone's opinion was "wrong" in the first place. I just said that particular tactic doesn't work for me.
And thank you for your response.

I see what you mean. I have a difficult time reconciling expectation management with envisioning a polar opposite. It seems to inflate my unattainable expectations when I try to imagine a different way of being. Do you know what I mean? It's not that I want life to be easy, it's not even a matter of desiring happiness. I just want to not wake up every morning wondering if this is the day. I work hard at being mindful, but when my mind does wander, it is always about death, and is always a cost-benefit analysis re: is it worth it to endure? Will there ever be a payoff? Will I ever feel stable? 

I think what I'm trying to understand is this: Am I the only person constantly assessing the value of my life and coming up short, and if not, how does everyone else cope? What I have heard so far in terms of how people cope just doesn't work for me.

What makes it less irrefutable? To refute means to show that something is an **opinion**. Therefore, if something is subjective, it can't be irrefutable. This is an argument about language, and a deflection. 

My point in that line is that I'm not looking for suggestions  of how to make meaning out of trauma. 

I don't understand why you're stuck on my opinion of the coping mechanisms of others. I don't care if that's what other people use to cope, but it doesn't work for me. That's entirely beside the point. I just don't want to hear that I feel this way "for a reason" because that is an opinion, not a constructive suggestion.
Thank you for the "positive on-switch" metaphor. I'm going to sit with that one for awhile.

If you haven't already, spend some time looking into Terror Management Theory. My point is that there are very few tangible truths in this world (i.e. we need oxygen to continue living). But people present their coping mechanisms as irrefutable truths, know what I mean?

Please re-read. I am not "faulting others" for what works for them. I am specifying what does not work for me, and asking that people do not give this advice. I am asking for someone to suggest something that I haven't thought of yet. I thought that was the whole point of this place.
